headline: Gohar refutes reports of Imran welcoming end of K-P government
description: Says all PTI lawmakers in K-P remain loyal to Imran, dismisses reports of a forward bloc within the party
author: Web Desk
article_text:
PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan on Tuesday rejected media reports suggesting that party founder Imran Khan had welcomed the end of the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa government, saying he had made no such statement during his meeting at Adiala jail with Barrister Salman Safdar.

On October 11, Governor's rule and an emergency were imposed, transferring executive authority from the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf-led provincial government to the governor. An 11-member advisory council was formed to assist him in overseeing provincial administrative affairs.

The federal government also established a separate administrative structure for 12 districts, including an Area Representative and Development Council to facilitate local representation and development planning.

Gohar's denial follows a meeting a day earlier between Barrister Safdar, the incarcerated PTI founder, and his wife, Bushra Bibi, to discuss a legal case.

The Islamabad High Court (IHC) has permitted Imran to meet his family members, lawyers and other associates twice a week, on Tuesdays and Thursdays. However, despite repeated court orders directing the authorities to allow these meetings, access to the former prime minister by his family and party leaders has remained largely restricted in recent months.

Speaking to reporters in Rawalpindi, Gohar said a television channel had incorrectly reported that Imran was pleased with the provincial government’s removal. “This is wrong. Khan did not say anything of the sort,” he said.

“One point I want to categorically reject is the claim made by a TV channel that Khan Sahib had welcomed the end of his government in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. That report is entirely false,” Gohar said.

He said all PTI members of the provincial assembly remained loyal to Imran and there was no forward bloc within the party. Any decision about the provincial government or a possible candidate for the chief minister’s office would be taken by the party founder, he added.

“Everyone will act according to Imran’s views. No one can suddenly come forward and say that he wants to form a government or become a candidate,” Gohar said, adding that the decision rested with the PTI founder and no one else.

He welcomed Safdar’s meeting with Imran, saying restrictions on access to the PTI founder had fuelled political tensions.

The PTI chairman said Safdar’s interaction with Imran was the first since April 8, following an extended period during which meetings with the former prime minister had remained restricted.

He said the political situation might have taken a different turn if such meetings had been permitted, adding that tensions could have been eased before matters escalated to the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Gohar said the party had repeatedly sought to arrange meetings with Imran, including requests for access for himself and Senate opposition leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas. After these efforts failed, the party worked to secure a meeting for Safdar with the former prime minister, he added.

Asked about the possibility of an alliance with the Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam after the end of governor’s rule, he said the party would consider the matter when the situation arose.

Gohar also rejected reports about Imran’s possible transfer from Adiala jail to Islamabad or Bani Gala, saying no such proposal had been discussed during the meeting.

Concern over Imran’s health

The PTI chairman said the party remained concerned about the founder’s health and conditions in prison, reiterating the party’s demand that the former prime minister be examined by a private doctor, undergo medical tests and receive treatment.

“We have not given up on this demand. It is an order of the Supreme Court, and it should be implemented,” he said.

Gohar said the party had raised concerns about Imran’s health and living conditions, adding that the meeting was important for the PTI as well as its legal team.

He added that the meeting with the PTI founder was the first in more than 380 days, describing the prolonged restrictions on meetings as inhuman treatment that had contributed to political tensions in the country.

Gohar said restrictions on meetings with the former prime minister’s family were particularly troubling, citing the case of a woman in prison who was not being allowed to meet her daughter.

“Even an ordinary prisoner has the right to meet family members,” he said, adding that such meetings were a legal right and should be allowed in accordance with court orders.

Gohar said meetings should be permitted with Imran’s lawyers, family members, doctors and children, as well as with the family of his wife.

He said the Supreme Court had issued orders in this regard and urged the authorities to implement them. Referring to an order issued on Aug 18, he said its implementation could have prevented the need for further intervention by the apex court and subsequent contempt proceedings.

He also said regular meetings could have helped ease political tensions and that, had they been allowed, the situation might not have escalated to the point of an emergency and governor’s rule in K-P.

Responding to questions about the political situation, Gohar said the party was concerned about what he described as growing political victimisation. He said people were increasingly feeling that they had no place in the system.

He also criticised the continued imprisonment of Imran’s three sisters, saying their detention was contrary to the country’s traditions. He said he had raised the issue in the provincial assembly and during media interactions, and expressed hope that a solution would be found.

Imran’s sisters — Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Uzma Khan — who frequently staged sit-ins outside Adiala jail demanding the PTI founder’s release, have remained in detention since late September under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, as the party prepared to stage a protest march towards Islamabad.

On JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s political position, Gohar said Imran had made it clear that Fazl had his own party and political agenda, with which the PTI had nothing to do.

He said he had advised Maulana Fazl to avoid certain remarks during their interaction, adding that the government had also responded inappropriately. "Political differences should not prevent efforts to strengthen the democratic system," he said.

Gohar said the PTI was continuing its efforts through the All Parties Conference to address the country’s political challenges.

Asked about reports that he had been considered for a meeting with political leaders but had not attended, he rejected the claim, saying he had consistently tried to arrange meetings with political figures, including Maulana Fazl and other leaders.

He said he had also made efforts to meet Safdar and was pleased that the meeting with the PTI founder had finally taken place.

Gohar said a case concerning the K-P chief minister, the speaker and a lawmaker was pending before the Peshawar High Court. He welcomed the chief justice’s decision to constitute a larger bench but urged the court to act swiftly.

“It is unbelievable that a minister and the speaker can disappear. Everyone should have responded, and the court should have taken up the matter as soon as possible,” he said.

article_html:
PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan on Tuesday rejected media reports suggesting that party founder Imran Khan had welcomed the end of the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa government, saying he had made no such statement during his meeting at Adiala jail with Barrister Salman Safdar.

On October 11, Governor's rule and an emergency were imposed, transferring executive authority from the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf-led provincial government to the governor. An 11-member advisory council was formed to assist him in overseeing provincial administrative affairs.

The federal government also established a separate administrative structure for 12 districts, including an Area Representative and Development Council to facilitate local representation and development planning.

Gohar's denial follows a meeting a day earlier between Barrister Safdar, the incarcerated PTI founder, and his wife, Bushra Bibi, to discuss a legal case.

The Islamabad High Court (IHC) has permitted Imran to meet his family members, lawyers and other associates twice a week, on Tuesdays and Thursdays. However, despite repeated court orders directing the authorities to allow these meetings, access to the former prime minister by his family and party leaders has remained largely restricted in recent months.

Read: JI questions PTI's lack of protests over governor's rule

Speaking to reporters in Rawalpindi, Gohar said a television channel had incorrectly reported that Imran was pleased with the provincial government’s removal. “This is wrong. Khan did not say anything of the sort,” he said.

“One point I want to categorically reject is the claim made by a TV channel that Khan Sahib had welcomed the end of his government in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. That report is entirely false,” Gohar said.

He said all PTI members of the provincial assembly remained loyal to Imran and there was no forward bloc within the party. Any decision about the provincial government or a possible candidate for the chief minister’s office would be taken by the party founder, he added.

“Everyone will act according to Imran’s views. No one can suddenly come forward and say that he wants to form a government or become a candidate,” Gohar said, adding that the decision rested with the PTI founder and no one else.

He welcomed Safdar’s meeting with Imran, saying restrictions on access to the PTI founder had fuelled political tensions.

The PTI chairman said Safdar’s interaction with Imran was the first since April 8, following an extended period during which meetings with the former prime minister had remained restricted.

He said the political situation might have taken a different turn if such meetings had been permitted, adding that tensions could have been eased before matters escalated to the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Gohar said the party had repeatedly sought to arrange meetings with Imran, including requests for access for himself and Senate opposition leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas. After these efforts failed, the party worked to secure a meeting for Safdar with the former prime minister, he added.

Asked about the possibility of an alliance with the Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam after the end of governor’s rule, he said the party would consider the matter when the situation arose.

Gohar also rejected reports about Imran’s possible transfer from Adiala jail to Islamabad or Bani Gala, saying no such proposal had been discussed during the meeting.

Concern over Imran’s health

The PTI chairman said the party remained concerned about the founder’s health and conditions in prison, reiterating the party’s demand that the former prime minister be examined by a private doctor, undergo medical tests and receive treatment.

“We have not given up on this demand. It is an order of the Supreme Court, and it should be implemented,” he said.

Gohar said the party had raised concerns about Imran’s health and living conditions, adding that the meeting was important for the PTI as well as its legal team.

He added that the meeting with the PTI founder was the first in more than 380 days, describing the prolonged restrictions on meetings as inhuman treatment that had contributed to political tensions in the country.

Gohar said restrictions on meetings with the former prime minister’s family were particularly troubling, citing the case of a woman in prison who was not being allowed to meet her daughter.

“Even an ordinary prisoner has the right to meet family members,” he said, adding that such meetings were a legal right and should be allowed in accordance with court orders.

Also Read: PHC seeks replies from governor, speaker against governor’s rule

Gohar said meetings should be permitted with Imran’s lawyers, family members, doctors and children, as well as with the family of his wife.

He said the Supreme Court had issued orders in this regard and urged the authorities to implement them. Referring to an order issued on Aug 18, he said its implementation could have prevented the need for further intervention by the apex court and subsequent contempt proceedings.

He also said regular meetings could have helped ease political tensions and that, had they been allowed, the situation might not have escalated to the point of an emergency and governor’s rule in K-P.

Responding to questions about the political situation, Gohar said the party was concerned about what he described as growing political victimisation. He said people were increasingly feeling that they had no place in the system.

He also criticised the continued imprisonment of Imran’s three sisters, saying their detention was contrary to the country’s traditions. He said he had raised the issue in the provincial assembly and during media interactions, and expressed hope that a solution would be found.

Imran’s sisters — Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Uzma Khan — who frequently staged sit-ins outside Adiala jail demanding the PTI founder’s release, have remained in detention since late September under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, as the party prepared to stage a protest march towards Islamabad.

On JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s political position, Gohar said Imran had made it clear that Fazl had his own party and political agenda, with which the PTI had nothing to do.

He said he had advised Maulana Fazl to avoid certain remarks during their interaction, adding that the government had also responded inappropriately. "Political differences should not prevent efforts to strengthen the democratic system," he said.

Gohar said the PTI was continuing its efforts through the All Parties Conference to address the country’s political challenges.

Asked about reports that he had been considered for a meeting with political leaders but had not attended, he rejected the claim, saying he had consistently tried to arrange meetings with political figures, including Maulana Fazl and other leaders.

Read More: Governor's rule to end after six months, NA told

He said he had also made efforts to meet Safdar and was pleased that the meeting with the PTI founder had finally taken place.

Gohar said a case concerning the K-P chief minister, the speaker and a lawmaker was pending before the Peshawar High Court. He welcomed the chief justice’s decision to constitute a larger bench but urged the court to act swiftly.

“It is unbelievable that a minister and the speaker can disappear. Everyone should have responded, and the court should have taken up the matter as soon as possible,” he said.

headline: IHC grants TikToker Anser Mahmood protective bail in wedding stampede case
description: Case has been registered against Mahmood in Sialkot on charges of culpable homicide, unlawful assembly and rioting
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Tuesday granted protective bail to TikToker Anser Mahmood, alias "Mr Patlu", who was nominated in a case registered over culpable homicide, unlawful assembly, rioting and the death of one person and injuries to several others in a stampede.

A prize draw at a TikToker's wedding celebration on Sunday turned deadly after a stampede at Faraz Ground in Daska left two people dead and 17 others injured.

The court directed the suspect to approach the relevant court by November 10. Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar heard the protective bail petition filed by Mahmood. The petitioner arrived at the court in a wheelchair, accompanied by his counsel, Barrister Qasim Nawaz Abbasi.

The petition stated that a case had been registered against him at the Motra Police Station in Sialkot district on charges of culpable homicide, unlawful assembly and rioting, following an incident in which one person was killed and several others were injured in a stampede.

The petitioner argued that the IHC had the authority to grant protective bail to enable him to approach the relevant court for pre-arrest bail without examining the merits of the case. Accepting the request, the court granted him protective bail until November 10.

On Sunday, a crowd had gathered for Mahmood's mehndi ceremony, after he had announced a prize draw featuring cars, motorcycles and cash rewards to attract participants and publicise the event.

The rush at the entrance gate triggered a stampede, during which several people fell to the ground and were trampled underfoot.

One of the victims, Aqeel, a resident of Budha Goraya, died at the scene, while 18 people were initially injured and shifted to hospitals. Among the injured was Rehan, a resident of Glotian Kalan, whose condition was critical.

He was referred to Lahore's Mayo Hospital but later succumbed to his injuries, taking the death toll to two and leaving 17 others injured.

Police registered a case at Motra Police Station on their own complaint under Sections 322, 431, 440, 188, 109, 148 and 149 of the Pakistan Penal Code, along with Section 16 of the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance.

The first information report named nine people, including Mahmood, Kashif, ground owner Haji Shahid Javed and other organisers Daniyal, Munir Ahmed, Mohsin Ali, Irshad Ali, Abdullah and Zohaib Mansha. Another 40 to 45 unidentified security guards had also been included in the case.

headline: Trump says US is close to making a trade deal with Canada
description: US-Canada tariffs emerge as an election issue in border states ahead of Tuesday's midterms
author: Reuters
article_text:
President Donald Trump said on ​Tuesday the United States was close ‌to making a trade deal with Canada.

"Canada is very good, we're going to ​make a deal with Canada ​very soon. We're going to make ⁠a great deal," Trump said ​in an interview with Fox News.

Canada and ​the United States have slapped billions of dollars in tariffs on each other in ​recent months. The imposition of ​tariffs on Canada has emerged as an issue ‌in ⁠some northern US border states like Michigan and Maine before US midterm elections on Tuesday.

Trump and Canadian Prime Minister ​Mark ​Carney said on ⁠Sunday they had spoken about a trade deal, which the ​US president said would be "great ​for ⁠our farmers".

Carney said on X: "Our teams will now be working in ⁠the ​coming weeks to deliver ​that outcome."

Carney and Trump had discussed the framework of a new bilateral trade agreement in a series of phone calls, signalling a possible breakthrough in resolving a months-long cross-border trade dispute.

Trump had also emphasised that the arrangement would dismantle Canadian agricultural trade barriers, asserting that "our farmers were paying tremendous tariffs to send things to Canada", reaching up to 400% on dairy items.

"All those tariffs will be gone. There will be no tariff," he maintained.

Outlining key provisions of the emerging accord, Trump said Ottawa agreed to finance the cross-border Keystone oil pipeline system connecting Canada and the US.

"They're going to build the Keystone Pipeline. They're going to pay for it," he noted, adding that Washington had largely determined the pipeline's transit route.

headline: IHC issues notices on plea seeking criminal proceedings in PIMS nursery fire
description: Court suspends order dismissing plea for registration of FIR over deaths of 15 children
author: Fiaz Mahmood
article_text:
The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Tuesday issued notices to the federal government and others in a petition seeking registration of a case over the deaths of children in the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) tragedy and compensation for the affected families.

Fourteen newborn babies were killed on August 26 after a fire broke out on the third floor of the Mother and Child Hospital’s ward at the PIMS hospital, while another child died later on September 17.

The notices were issued to the Prime Minister’s Office, Ministry of Health, Establishment Division, Islamabad Healthcare Regulatory Authority, Auditor General, chief commissioner, deputy commissioner, Capital Development Authority, Capital Emergency Services, PIMS executive director, Islamabad inspector general of Police and Federal Investigation Agency director general.

The court also summoned the complete record, including the inquiry report into the incident, and suspended an order passed by a justice of the peace dismissing an application for registration of an FIR.

Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro heard the petition filed by lawyer Riaz Hanif Rahi.

The petitioner told the court that 14 children had caught fire simultaneously in the PIMS incident, while another child died later. He said no FIR had been registered to date over the deaths.

The court asked whether an inquiry had been conducted into the incident. In response, Rahi said the inquiry report had established negligence.

He requested the court to direct the authorities to register an FIR immediately and submit it before the court by the end of the day’s proceedings.

The petitioner further said the justice of peace had dismissed his application for registration of a case because petitions concerning the matter were already pending before the high court.

He maintained that, apart from him, no one had approached the police station with an application, and a case should have been registered. He questioned the purpose of collecting evidence when no criminal case had been registered to pursue the matter.

The court observed that it would summon all reports and evidence and, if negligence was established, direct the registration of cases against those responsible.

After issuing notices to the respondents, the court adjourned further proceedings until November 12.

An inquiry committee presented its interim report to the premier on August 29, which led to the suspension of eight high-ranking officers from PIMS and external agencies, with disciplinary proceedings initiated against them. It also recommended a civil and monetary award for Nurse Razia, who saved a newborn from the fire, while placing the charge nurse and security guard off duty.

On September 15, the inquiry committee constituted by the prime minister to investigate the PIMS fire concluded that the tragedy culminated as a result of “systemic and institutional failures”, with the hospital and its senior management bearing primary responsibility for failing to address known safety risks.

The report, based on a 52-point investigation, found that multiple safety measures were either absent, inadequate, not activated in time or had never been independently verified.

The committee concluded that criminal responsibility of an individual would have to be determined separately under the relevant rules and on the basis of available evidence.

It placed primary institutional responsibility on PIMS and its senior management for failing to convert known risks and earlier warnings into an effective safety system.

The inquiry committee recommended immediate fire-safety measures and a comprehensive electrical-safety audit at PIMS. It called for effective fire-detection, alarm, firefighting and evacuation systems, along with dedicated SOPs for newborn evacuation and realistic fire and evacuation drills.

headline: Living in digital darkness
description: Living in digital darkness
author: Mujeeb Ali
article_text:
We are living in the 21st century - an era of unprecedented technological advancement and digital transformation, where AI, social media and smartphones have revolutionised the way we communicate, learn, work and access information.

From the Industrial Revolution to today's digital revolution, technology has dramatically improved living standards. It has transformed industries, simplified everyday tasks, increased productivity and connected billions of people across the globe. Today, digital tools are indispensable in education, healthcare, business, governance and scientific research. From daily wage labourers using mobile banking to professionals working remotely, technology has become an integral part of modern life.

The world has digitally connected, but has created a wide disconnect in human relationships. People are connected on social media just for the sake of appearances, and they are unaware of their neighbours. Ironically, they have hundreds of friends on social media platforms but hardly know about them. They consume hours scrolling through reels and videos, wasting valuable time and energy. When it is time to spend with family members or friends, they often make excuses, saying that they are too busy.

Not long ago, families and friends regularly gathered to share meals, visit one another, and spend quality time together. Nowadays, it is increasingly common to see people sitting in the same room absorbed in their smartphones. Conversations are interrupted by endless scrolling through social media platforms. Although we are constantly "connected", genuine human interaction is steadily declining.

An estimated 35 million children in Pakistan are now online, many of them without adequate supervision. Pakistani children spend almost 43% of their screen time on YouTube, followed by 16% on WhatsApp and nearly 9% on Instagram. At the same time, internet-based crimes against children are rising rapidly. Parents are frequently unaware of the type of content their children consume online. Many children create accounts on Instagram and TikTok and upload content without any parental oversight or verification of whether it is appropriate, informative or beneficial.

Many young people imitate online influencers in pursuit of likes, followers and instant fame, often at the expense of their cultural values, personal dignity, and even their safety. Privacy has also become increasingly vulnerable as users routinely share personal information without fully understanding the consequences. According to PEMRA, Pakistanis spent over $689 million on digital media in 2024, including $158 million on video games. In 2025, expenditure on video-on-demand services reached $392 million, with a substantial share reportedly spent on adult content.

Since children have highly impressionable minds, prolonged exposure to low-quality or inappropriate content can negatively influence their behaviour, language, values and personality. Furthermore, screen time is increasingly replacing the time they would otherwise spend interacting with parents, siblings and friends.

Aristotle famously said, "Man is by nature a social animal." The problem is not merely psychological; it is also sociological. Human beings learn brotherhood, cooperation, communication and emotional intelligence through face-to-face interaction.

This does not mean that technology itself is the problem. Digital connectivity has brought remarkable progress that should be embraced as a means of survival.

Challenge lies in the effective implementation of the Social Media (Age Restriction for Users) Act. Countries such as the UK, Australia and New Zealand have imposed restrictions on social media access for children under the age of 16. Pakistan has also adopted a similar approach, but it requires stronger enforcement and a comprehensive regulatory framework to ensure its effectiveness. Schools should teach digital citizenship alongside digital literacy, enabling students to use technology responsibly, safely and ethically.

headline: Adiala breakthrough
description: Adiala breakthrough
author: editorial
article_text:
In a breakthrough of sorts in the legal realm, PTI lawyer Barrister Salman Safdar met Imran Khan and his spouse, Bushra Bibi, in Adiala jail after a hiatus spanning months. This sudden meeting has come as a pleasant surprise for party members and supporters. Safdar, as amicus curiae of the Supreme Court, had earlier twice met the incarcerated former prime minister, aprising the court of his health and jail conditions.

Given to understand that the reputed lawyer is a thorough professional, who has kept himself away from any narrative building, there is not much to read in the political context. Nonetheless, the meeting happening out of the blue after a prolonged solitary confinement has surely raised hope for a fall in political temperature. This move can be built upon to provide due relief to the former first couple and, likewise, to all political prisoners, thereby addressing the pestering political stability in the country.

The Monday meet must lead to regularisation of meetings with the imprisoned political leaders as per the jail manual. The defiance of the government to restrict lawful audiences with family, lawyers and personal physicians despite standing court orders had not only caused friction among the organs of the state, but also deepened mistrust in the sitting dispensation. The courts too failed to assert their writ, especially after the controversial 26th and 27th constitutional amendments – proving to be detrimental in the process of speedy justice and timely relief.

The way forward is to ensure that cases pending for appeal and bails see the light of the day. Imran Khan too had prescribed such a modus operandi, and the party has been continuously knocking on the doors of the court. The tendency of the executive overseeing the judiciary must come to an end, and justice be dispensed as per law and the Constitution. No out-of-the-box solution is desired for putting an end to political instability, as all it entails is to let the law take its course.

headline: Fuel relief
description: Fuel relief
author: editorial
article_text:
The government's latest effort to bring down fuel prices revises the petrol pricing mechanism by asking oil refineries to absorb the difference between import and ex-refinery prices through a petroleum levy. But while the immediate effect is expected to lower prices, the move carries several potential risks, raising concerns among analysts.

Unfortunately, the government is running out of options, and with the US-Israeli war on Iran sending international prices soaring, there are only a few measures available to keep the prices down without trampling on the bottom lines of fuel companies. The new arrangement, approved by the federal cabinet on Oct 30, will see refineries surrender the price differential, allowing petrol to be sold Rs15 cheaper than global market rates and sparing motorists a punishing blow. The measure will, in theory, also help reduce inflation, as prices depend on transportation costs, which are directly tied to fuel prices.

With refineries collectively bearing a burden of approximately Rs15 billion each month, this additional load could push gross refining margins into negative territory. Industry officials argue the policy was changed without prior consultation, forcing them to sell petrol below production cost and creating regulatory uncertainty that may discourage future investment. The government's own figures reportedly put the surrender at Rs49 per litre, which is significantly higher than the Rs15 number being thrown around. The government's justification is largely based on the fact that oil companies have earned excess profits due to price fluctuations in recent months.

But even though oil companies are rarely deserving of anyone's sympathy, they do have a valid complaint in that the difference between import and ex-factory prices is not all profit, and converting the entire amount into a levy is effectively forcing them to operate at a loss due to the failure to account for salaries, overheads and other expenses. Reducing prices at the pump is useful, but it is a short-term goal. A better strategy would have been to heavily tax the excess profits and use the funds to bridge budget gaps.

headline: Polio protection
description: Polio protection
author: editorial
article_text:
Pakistan's struggle against polio is being undermined not only by the persistence of the virus but also by the violence directed at those working to eradicate it. Two policemen were recently killed and another injured in an attack on personnel assigned to polio vaccination duty in K-P's Mohmand district. Such attacks threaten the lives of frontline workers and jeopardise efforts to protect children from a disease that much of the world has already eliminated.

Compounding the problem are the myths and misconceptions surrounding polio vaccination, which continue to fuel mistrust and vaccine refusals. False claims about infertility and the safety of vaccines have prevented many parents from immunising their children, leaving them vulnerable to a preventable disease. The government must counter these misconceptions through sustained awareness campaigns involving religious scholars, community leaders and healthcare professionals to educate the public and build confidence in vaccination. However, the government has a major responsibility to ensure that vaccination workers and the police personnel protecting them are not left vulnerable to armed attacks. Personnel operating in high-risk districts should be provided with appropriate protective equipment, including ballistic vests and helmets where the threat assessment warrants them to. The authorities must also investigate attacks promptly and ensure that those responsible are brought to justice.

Eradicating polio requires a sustained commitment to public trust and the safety of those carrying out vaccination campaigns. The government must recognise that misinformation and insecurity are serious obstacles to immunisation, and both demand a coordinated response. Vaccination teams cannot be expected to fulfil their responsibilities while risking their lives, nor can Pakistan afford to allow preventable infections to continue because parents remain misinformed. Protecting frontline workers and educating communities must become central to the country's eradication strategy.

headline: Lancet report and Pakistan's public health crisis
description: Lancet report and Pakistan's public health crisis
author: Dr Rana Jawad Asghar
article_text:
When I moved back to Pakistan, I had never imagined the scale of our health challenges. Having worked in some of the poorest countries in Africa, I assumed that Pakistan would be much better on different indicators. Unfortunately, every passing year we fall behind on health indicators compared to many poorer countries. Wild polio has been eradicated from all over the world even from war-torn countries, except for Pakistan and Afghanistan. In Pakistan, according to WHO, every single day 675 newborns and 27 mothers die in childbirth. Pakistan's maternal mortality rate is highest in South Asia when compared with India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

One of the world's top medical journals, The Lancet has published "The 2026 Global Report of the Lancet Countdown", documenting how climate change is affecting our health. It is a separate discussion as to who is responsible for climate degradation and how much they should be held responsible for financial compensation. We must now think about safeguarding our already vulnerable population from increased health risks due to climate degradation.

According to this report, the number of moderate or higher heat stress hours has increased significantly in both Pakistan and India (more than 2000 hours/year), costing Pakistan $17 billion and India $174 billion (of course, due to its larger population and economy). Increased heat is also increasing favourable months for transmission of mosquito-borne diseases like malaria and dengue. This year though our underreporting of dengue is showing few dengue cases. However, I myself was recently infected by dengue even though I was always meticulous about protecting myself. There is a limit to individual preventive measures if infectious diseases are not being controlled at the population level.

Climate change is also bringing extreme floods and droughts in the region. In Pakistan, the 2022 floods damaged around 1,500 health facilities. Thirty-five percent of Pakistan's land has experienced extreme drought annually for the last many years.

According to the same report, air pollution is now one of the major challenges, costing India $500 billion and Pakistan $33 billion. These numbers should alert decision-makers, even if we don't talk about the immense health costs of air pollution. A 2030% increase in mortality from heart diseases, cancers and strokes is linked to air pollution. This year too both Indian and Pakistani cities are occupying four to five top slots in the top ten most polluted cities in the world.

The Lancet report suggests some priority actions. First, consider the consequences of climate change like health emergencies, and start preparing for them. Since frequent floods and droughts are now part of regular cycles, be prepared. Build resilience by making sure there are flood-resilient health facilities with solar electricity and cold chains for vaccinations. Deploy mobile health services to operate in natural emergencies. Establish a real-time, representative and effective disease surveillance and response system.

These are important steps to prepare for climate-induced health emergencies. But unless we address the core issues of our public health - such as population growth, safe drinking water and nutrition - our preparedness for emergencies will only be tinkering at the edges.

Pakistan is an agricultural country, but 40% of our children are stunted. Severe malnutrition may reduce 10 to 15 IQ points in children. Over the decades, successive governments did nothing to improve the situation.

Pakistan's fertility rate is around 3.5 while every other country in South Asia has a fertility rate of around 2 or lower. Our population explosion is now threatening national security as we can't provide food, health and education for our children. Our population is already physically and mentally disadvantaged, and the fast-approaching climate health crisis will affect us even more. We were already struggling with uncontrolled infectious diseases and non-communicable diseases, and this climate-related health emergency now completes a triple whammy of health crises.

We need to strengthen our foundations while still repairing our roof for the incoming rains.

article_html:
When I moved back to Pakistan, I had never imagined the scale of our health challenges. Having worked in some of the poorest countries in Africa, I assumed that Pakistan would be much better on different indicators. Unfortunately, every passing year we fall behind on health indicators compared to many poorer countries. Wild polio has been eradicated from all over the world even from war-torn countries, except for Pakistan and Afghanistan. In Pakistan, according to WHO, every single day 675 newborns and 27 mothers die in childbirth. Pakistan's maternal mortality rate is highest in South Asia when compared with India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

One of the world's top medical journals, The Lancet has published "The 2026 Global Report of the Lancet Countdown", documenting how climate change is affecting our health. It is a separate discussion as to who is responsible for climate degradation and how much they should be held responsible for financial compensation. We must now think about safeguarding our already vulnerable population from increased health risks due to climate degradation.

According to this report, the number of moderate or higher heat stress hours has increased significantly in both Pakistan and India (more than 2000 hours/year), costing Pakistan $17 billion and India $174 billion (of course, due to its larger population and economy). Increased heat is also increasing favourable months for transmission of mosquito-borne diseases like malaria and dengue. This year though our underreporting of dengue is showing few dengue cases. However, I myself was recently infected by dengue even though I was always meticulous about protecting myself. There is a limit to individual preventive measures if infectious diseases are not being controlled at the population level.

Climate change is also bringing extreme floods and droughts in the region. In Pakistan, the 2022 floods damaged around 1,500 health facilities. Thirty-five percent of Pakistan's land has experienced extreme drought annually for the last many years.

According to the same report, air pollution is now one of the major challenges, costing India $500 billion and Pakistan $33 billion. These numbers should alert decision-makers, even if we don't talk about the immense health costs of air pollution. A 2030% increase in mortality from heart diseases, cancers and strokes is linked to air pollution. This year too both Indian and Pakistani cities are occupying four to five top slots in the top ten most polluted cities in the world.

Since frequent floods and droughts are now part of regular cycles, be prepared. Build resilience by making sure there are flood-resilient health facilities with solar electricity and cold chains for vaccinations. Deploy mobile health services to operate in natural emergencies. Establish a real-time, representative and effective disease surveillance and response system.

These are important steps to prepare for climate-induced health emergencies. But unless we address the core issues of our public health - such as population growth, safe drinking water and nutrition - our preparedness for emergencies will only be tinkering at the edges.

headline: The shifting scales of global power
description: The shifting scales of global power
author: Asad Ashraf Malik
article_text:
The world stands at the threshold of a historic transformation, as the old architecture of global power trembles. For decades, the United States occupied the commanding heights of military supremacy. Yet history is an impatient sculptor; empires cannot retain their familiar contours forever. China's rise is redrawing global influence and forcing Washington to confront a once-unthinkable question: can American power still dictate another great power's ambitions?

China's ascent is no longer merely an economic miracle. It is visible in technological innovation, military modernisation, naval expansion, missile development, Artificial Intelligence and integrated warfare. This century's contest will not be measured simply by the number of aircraft, ships or missiles in rival arsenals, but by how intelligently they are woven into a single web of military power.

Modern warfare is no longer a collection of isolated battles. It is an intricate orchestra in which satellites, aircraft, ground forces, naval platforms, submarines and information networks must perform in harmony. Advantage belongs not necessarily to the nation with the largest arsenal, but to the one that sees first, decides faster and strikes precisely. Information is the eye, technology the nervous system, and coordination the invisible hand of military strength.

Pakistan's military cooperation with China illustrates this landscape. Collaboration in defence production, aviation and technology has strengthened its capabilities. Superiority in the skies cannot be divorced from intelligence in space, strength on land or command of the seas. The future belongs to integrated power, where separate instruments become a single, responsive shield.

The May 2025 India-Pakistan confrontation brought this transformation into sharp focus. Pakistan's response to India's opening strikes demonstrated the importance of coordination, intelligence, electronic warfare and modern air-combat systems. The Pakistan Air Force claimed to have brought down six Indian military aircraft, including three French-made Rafales. India subsequently acknowledged aerial losses, and its Chief of Staff conceded that aircraft had been lost in the engagements. Independent assessments also identified evidence of multiple Indian aircraft losses. The encounter challenged assumptions about the invulnerability of sophisticated Western platforms, showing how technology, intelligence and coordination can alter the balance in the skies. Pakistan's performance deserves neither patriotic exaggeration nor hostile denial, but sober examination: technological complacency carries a heavy price.

These developments complicate Washington's calculations. Direct confrontation between nuclear-armed powers would be catastrophic. Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan and now Iran remind us that military superiority does not guarantee victory against a determined adversary. The mightiest war machine may command the battlefield, yet remain imprisoned in history's unforgiving corridors.

When direct confrontation becomes prohibitively dangerous, rivalry does not disappear; it changes its clothing. The battlefield shifts, actors multiply, and principal contestants may advance their interests through regional partners and local conflicts. Thus emerges the perilous politics of proxy warfare: a shadowy contest in which distant powers pull the strings while smaller nations dance upon the edge of an abyss.

The Philippines occupies a sensitive position. Its proximity to China and importance in the South China Sea make it pivotal to the Indo-Pacific equation. Taiwan remains another combustible flashpoint. Turning either into an instrument of strategic coercion could transform regional disagreement into a conflagration far beyond Asia.

In proxy warfare, those who light the match are rarely first to feel its heat. Powerful capitals calculate advantages from fortified chambers, while soldiers, fishermen and families pay the price. The architects sit behind closed doors; debris falls upon villages, grief enters homes, and wounds pass through generations. Smaller nations must not mistake a patron's embrace for permanent security. A borrowed umbrella offers little protection in a hurricane.

India, Pakistan and South Asia must exercise restraint. Their rivalry is burdened by history, territorial disputes and nuclear risks. May's confrontation showed how rapidly modern weapons inflict damage and how consequences reverberate for generations. It should prompt sober examination of capabilities and vulnerabilities, not triumphalism. In the nuclear age, dignity lies not in bellicose rhetoric, but in preventing a passing storm from becoming catastrophe.

For Pakistan, the relationship with China remains important, but must be guided by mature diplomacy and national interests. Friendship should be a bridge to stability, not a passage into another country's confrontation. Pakistan can gain from technological cooperation, economic partnership and regional connectivity, but stands to lose if the subcontinent becomes a chessboard for distant powers, indifferent to those living on its squares.

The Philippines, too, is better served by diplomacy than by becoming the frontline of a contest between giants. Its sovereignty deserves respect, as do China's security concerns, which should be addressed through dialogue. Statesmanship means distinguishing firmness from belligerence and preventing disagreement from becoming destruction.

China's rise should not invite celebration of one power's decline or another's triumph. Replacing one hegemon with another would hardly herald peace. Humanity has paid dearly for imperial arrogance and those who mistook military strength for immortality. History's ruins are crowded with monuments to power, but painfully short of monuments to wisdom.

The United States and China must recognise that their rivalry cannot become humanity's collective misfortune. The South China Sea must not become a theatre of miscalculation, Taiwan the fuse of a global explosion, or South Asia another arena of confrontation.

The world needs fewer leaders who wear war upon their lips and more statesmen who carry peace in their hearts.

In the final reckoning, a powerful nation's greatest victory is not the destruction of its adversary, but the preservation of a world in which future generations can look towards the horizon without seeing war's dark silhouette hanging over their skies. Empires may rise upon the wings of power, but only wisdom can keep the world from falling beneath them.

headline: When Washington sanctions justice
description: When Washington sanctions justice
author: Faisal Kutty
article_text:
The United States helped establish the principle that leaders who commit atrocities should answer to judges. It is now demonstrating how a powerful country can punish the judges instead.

On October 9, the Trump administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court itself, escalating a campaign previously directed at its officials. The consequences extend beyond Washington's confrontation with The Hague. For countries that cannot enforce their interests through military or economic power, weakening international justice carries a particular danger.

International law offers no guarantee of protection. But a world in which courts operate only with powerful states' permission offers even less.

The sanctions require precise description. A US Treasury licence permits transactions necessary to maintain or wind down the court's operations through April 7, 2027. It expressly covers continued operations, including salaries, rent and routine services. Separate licences address specified technology, pension and detainee-related transactions. The institutional licence does not, by itself, authorise transactions involving sanctioned officials separately.

These permissions provide breathing space. They also expose the court's vulnerability: essential transactions depend on exceptions a government seeks to restrict. The sanctions create uncertainty for banks and suppliers and risk disrupting the services investigations depend on. Judicial independence becomes harder to sustain when foreign financial pressure targets the machinery needed to exercise it.

America's relationship with the ICC has long been selective. Its refusal to join did not prevent cooperation when the court pursued cases Washington supported. American officials publicly endorsed its work in Darfur, Libya and Ukraine. The United States also facilitated the transfer of Congolese commander Bosco Ntaganda to The Hague after he appeared at its embassy in Kigali.

That history complicates Washington's claim that the court lacks legitimacy. American officials have recognised its value when its work served objectives they supported.

Trump's February 2025 sanctions order made his administration's objection explicit: it rejected the court's actions against Americans and Israeli officials, including the arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant.

Those warrants concern alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, including starvation as a method of warfare. They are not convictions. Israel rejects the allegations and disputes the court's jurisdiction. Those distinctions matter because defending international justice requires respect for legal process, including the rights of the accused.

Jurisdictional objections deserve a legal hearing. Financial coercion cannot establish a court's lack of authority.

The administration argues that neither the United States nor Israel joined the Rome Statute. Yet nationality is not the only basis for criminal jurisdiction. States ordinarily prosecute foreigners for crimes committed on their territory. The ICC's framework likewise permits jurisdiction over qualifying crimes committed on the territory of a state party, including where the accused is a national of a non-member country.

In the Palestine situation, the court bases its territorial jurisdiction on Palestine's accession to the Rome Statute, its acceptance of jurisdiction and judicial rulings concerning the occupied Palestinian territory. Israel contests that jurisdiction. However, non-membership alone does not resolve the dispute.

The framework also prioritises national courts. Under complementarity, genuine domestic proceedings concerning the same person and substantially the same conduct can make an ICC case inadmissible. Sovereignty carries an opportunity to deliver justice at home.

For Pakistani readers, the issue should reach beyond whether Washington is being hypocritical. That charge is familiar. The more consequential question is what replaces the institutions it weakens.

If courts can effectively investigate only those without powerful protectors, international criminal law becomes a system for disciplining the vulnerable. If financial pressure can obstruct proceedings, control over banking influences whose claims can be heard.

The court deserves criticism. Its uneven reach, lengthy proceedings and dependence on state cooperation demand scrutiny. But crippling its capacity would leave victims with fewer options while preserving the advantages of powerful suspects.

Consistency must also govern support for the court. A government cannot credibly demand accountability for Palestinians while treating comparable allegations elsewhere as an inconvenience. The principle must survive changes in the accused's identity.

States that defend international justice should help preserve the court's access to banking, technology and essential services through lawful arrangements. They should challenge coercive measures through available legal and diplomatic channels while insisting on fair proceedings and accountability within the court itself.

Washington should contest disputed jurisdiction in court. Its economic power should not determine which victims can seek a hearing.

America's adversaries benefit when its conduct discredits its language of accountability. So does every leader seeking protection from scrutiny.

The greatest cost will fall on those without such protection.

cleaned_blocks.text: The United States helped establish the principle that leaders who commit atrocities should answer to judges. It is now demonstrating how a powerful country can punish the judges instead.

On October 9, the Trump administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court itself, escalating a campaign previously directed at its officials. The consequences extend beyond Washington's confrontation with The Hague. For countries that cannot enforce their interests through military or economic power, weakening international justice carries a particular danger.
International law offers no guarantee of protection. But a world in which courts operate only with powerful states' permission offers even less.

The sanctions require precise description. A US Treasury licence permits transactions necessary to maintain or wind down the court's operations through April 7, 2027. It expressly covers continued operations, including salaries, rent and routine services. Separate licences address specified technology, pension and detainee-related transactions. The institutional licence does not, by itself, authorise transactions involving sanctioned officials separately.

These permissions provide breathing space. They also expose the court's vulnerability: essential transactions depend on exceptions a government seeks to restrict. The sanctions create uncertainty for banks and suppliers and risk disrupting the services investigations depend on. Judicial independence becomes harder to sustain when foreign financial pressure targets the machinery needed to exercise it.

America's relationship with the ICC has long been selective. Its refusal to join did not prevent cooperation when the court pursued cases Washington supported. American officials publicly endorsed its work in Darfur, Libya and Ukraine. The United States also facilitated the transfer of Congolese commander Bosco Ntaganda to The Hague after he appeared at its embassy in Kigali.
That history complicates Washington's claim that the court lacks legitimacy. American officials have recognised its value when its work served objectives they supported.

Trump's February 2025 sanctions order made his administration's objection explicit: it rejected the court's actions against Americans and Israeli officials, including the arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant.

Those warrants concern alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, including starvation as a method of warfare. They are not convictions. Israel rejects the allegations and disputes the court's jurisdiction. Those distinctions matter because defending international justice requires respect for legal process, including the rights of the accused.
Jurisdictional objections deserve a legal hearing. Financial coercion cannot establish a court's lack of authority.

The administration argues that neither the United States nor Israel joined the Rome Statute. Yet nationality is not the only basis for criminal jurisdiction. States ordinarily prosecute foreigners for crimes committed on their territory. The ICC's framework likewise permits jurisdiction over qualifying crimes committed on the territory of a state party, including where the accused is a national of a non-member country.

In the Palestine situation, the court bases its territorial jurisdiction on Palestine's accession to the Rome Statute, its acceptance of jurisdiction and judicial rulings concerning the occupied Palestinian territory. Israel contests that jurisdiction. However, non-membership alone does not resolve the dispute.

The framework also prioritises national courts. Under complementarity, genuine domestic proceedings concerning the same person and substantially the same conduct can make an ICC case inadmissible. Sovereignty carries an opportunity to deliver justice at home.
For Pakistani readers, the issue should reach beyond whether Washington is being hypocritical. That charge is familiar. The more consequential question is what replaces the institutions it weakens.

If courts can effectively investigate only those without powerful protectors, international criminal law becomes a system for disciplining the vulnerable. If financial pressure can obstruct proceedings, control over banking influences whose claims can be heard.

The court deserves criticism. Its uneven reach, lengthy proceedings and dependence on state cooperation demand scrutiny. But crippling its capacity would leave victims with fewer options while preserving the advantages of powerful suspects.

Consistency must also govern support for the court. A government cannot credibly demand accountability for Palestinians while treating comparable allegations elsewhere as an inconvenience. The principle must survive changes in the accused's identity.

States that defend international justice should help preserve the court's access to banking, technology and essential services through lawful arrangements. They should challenge coercive measures through available legal and diplomatic channels while insisting on fair proceedings and accountability within the court itself.
Washington should contest disputed jurisdiction in court. Its economic power should not determine which victims can seek a hearing.
America's adversaries benefit when its conduct discredits its language of accountability. So does every leader seeking protection from scrutiny.
The greatest cost will fall on those without such protection.

headline: CM Maryam sends Rs 5b legal notices to Salik Hussain, TV channel over corruption remarks
description: Says Salik made sweeping corruption allegations without evidence, damaging her and provincial government’s reputation
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz has served a Rs5 billion defamation notice on Federal Minister Chaudhry Salik Hussain, an ARY News anchor and the private television channel's chairman, over allegations of widespread corruption in the province, demanding an unconditional apology, retraction of the statements and damages.

However, Salik Hussain, who belongs to a smaller allied party in the ruling coalition, has stood by his allegations, insisting that corruption was taking place in Punjab.

He has also rejected the suggestion that his remarks were prompted by the appointment of a deputy commissioner on merit, maintaining that the interview had been recorded three weeks earlier.

"If you have proof, bring it forward; if not, I will drag you to court," Maryam said during a laptop distribution ceremony, reiterating the allegation made a day earlier by Information Minister Azma Bukhari that the federal minister had effectively issued a charge sheet against the provincial government out of displeasure over the appointment of a deputy commissioner on merit.

A day earlier, Salik had acknowledged that he had indeed asked the government to appoint a deputy commissioner whose capabilities were better suited to executing mega projects.

During a talk show on a private television channel on Monday, Salik praised his paternal uncle, Chaudhry Pervez Elahi, president of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), for his tenure as Punjab chief minister from 2002 to 2007, saying he had overseen development across the province without political or personal bias.

“Chaudhry Pervez Elahi is the best chief executive Punjab has ever had,” he said, adding that the former chief minister had played a significant role in the province’s development and ensured that public projects were not influenced by political affiliations.

Salik also criticised the incumbent provincial government, alleging that political considerations were increasingly shaping development priorities and the allocation of public funds.

He said complaints about corruption in Punjab were commonplace, claiming that a disproportionate share of the provincial development budget was being spent in Lahore, while districts such as Gujrat, where candidates backed by the government had lost elections, were being overlooked in development planning.

Although Salik acknowledged that he did not possess evidence to substantiate his claims, he went on to say that corruption-related files had filled entire cupboards.

During the interview, the federal minister said: "I have no evidence, but I hear stories about corruption in Punjab every day." He also remarked that "cupboards are filled with files on corruption cases in Punjab".

The notices contend that Salik made sweeping allegations about corruption in Punjab without providing any evidence to substantiate them, damaging the reputation of the chief minister and the provincial administration.

According to the legal notice, the minister had referred to accounts of corruption in Punjab during the interview but failed to provide any documentary or verifiable evidence in support of his assertions.

The chief minister’s counsel said the remarks conveyed serious imputations that corruption was widespread in Punjab, that numerous corruption-related matters existed and that the provincial administration was burdened with a large volume of records relating to corruption.

The notice questioned the factual basis of Salik’s claims, asking which departments, public offices, officials, projects or transactions he was referring to, and whether his remarks were based on any complaints, inquiries, investigations or official records.

It said a federal minister was expected to appreciate the gravity and consequences of making such allegations against another constitutional government.

“The office of a federal minister is not a licence to circulate rumours, convert hearsay into apparent fact, or make sweeping accusations against another constitutional Government without identifying any credible factual basis,” the notice said.

It added that Salik had not identified a single authentic document, official inquiry, audit observation, investigation, complaint or other verifiable source to support his assertion that corruption-related files had filled entire cupboards in Punjab.

The notice argued that such sweeping remarks could create the impression among viewers that corruption was endemic throughout the provincial administration, rather than confined to isolated instances, and could not be shielded from legal scrutiny by describing them as political commentary.

The notices characterised the allegations as baseless, unverified and defamatory, arguing that Salik had failed to identify any specific incident, investigation or complaint during the interview to support his claims.

They also accused the programme host of broadcasting the allegations and facilitating discussion on the matter without first establishing their authenticity.

“The right to question a government cannot be converted into a right to manufacture or circulate damaging impressions without accepting responsibility for their factual basis,” the notice said, adding that the statements had crossed the permissible limits of responsible public discussion.

The chief minister maintained that the remarks had harmed the reputation of both herself and the Punjab government, prompting her to initiate legal proceedings against those responsible for making and broadcasting them.

Earlier, announcing her decision to issue the defamation notice, Maryam said she would not tolerate false allegations. She also challenged the federal minister to leave the government if he believed corruption was so widespread in Punjab.

She maintained that the actual issue was the appointment of a deputy commissioner in Gujrat rather than any development project.

She said she did not entertain requests or recommendations in the appointment of deputy commissioners, commissioners and regional police officers, insisting that all such appointments were made strictly on merit. Those appointed through influence, she added, ended up harming the country.

Rejecting the federal minister's assessment of Chaudhry Pervaiz Elahi as the best chief minister, Maryam said that when she assumed office, Gujrat resembled a village, with rainfall submerging the entire city and forcing people to travel not in cars but on trolleys.

Referring to her own visit to the city, she said she had undertaken development projects worth billions of rupees and could be held accountable for even a penny's worth of corruption.

It is pertinent to mention that Salik Hussain's brother, Chaudhry Shafay Hussain, is also part of the provincial government and serves directly under Maryam Nawaz as Punjab's minister for industries, commerce and investment.

Responding to the allegations against him, Federal Minister Chaudhry Salik Hussain said he had merely answered the interviewer's questions honestly, reiterating his position that corruption existed in Punjab.

However, he sidestepped questions about whether he possessed any evidence to support his allegations or whether he should leave the government if corruption was indeed taking place in the province.

Taking an indirect swipe at Maryam Nawaz, he said people holding powerful positions should remain humble.

"May Allah save people from pride and arrogance," he added.

Bokhari's rebuttal

The remarks also drew an immediate response from Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari, who suggested that Salik’s criticism stemmed from personal resentment over a favour being refused rather than a principled objection to the government’s policies.

She claimed that Salik had been displeased after his request to have a deputy commissioner of his choice appointed was turned down.

“Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz does not appoint deputy commissioners on anyone’s recommendation. She makes decisions strictly on merit and in line with the government’s policy,” Bokhari said.

Maintaining that the chief minister had ended the practice of political patronage, personal preferences and recommendations, she said influential individuals could no longer use their political connections to secure government appointments or administrative favours.

“There is no room for land grabbers and strongmen in Punjab anymore. The practice of rewarding employees of political estates with government positions through recommendations has also come to an end. Salik Hussain should not bite the hand that feeds him,” she retorted.

Bokhari also rejected Salik’s allegations of unequal development spending, saying Maryam Nawaz had ensured a transparent and equitable distribution of provincial resources, with similar development schemes being launched in cities across Punjab.

She said the sanitation model introduced in Lahore had also been extended to rural areas, arguing that the provincial government was pursuing development beyond the provincial capital instead of concentrating resources in one city.

Responding to Salik’s criticism of the use of official aircraft, Bokhari said Maryam Nawaz was the first Punjab chief minister to personally bear the expenses incurred through the use of the government aircraft.

She also cited an allocation of Rs12 billion for development projects in Gujrat, describing it as an unprecedented investment in the city’s history.

headline: Ishrat's reforms yet to be implemented
description: Ishrat's reforms yet to be implemented
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
December 1999, Pakistan had been left with only $300 million in foreign exchange reserves due to crippling economic sanctions and international isolation and at that time military ruler General Pervez Musharraf appointed Dr Ishrat Husain to turn around the central bank.

Six years later, when he left, the country had $13 billion in foreign exchange reserves, also built by purchasing dollars, and people's trust in banks and in the economy had been restored.

The $300 million reserves that Pakistan had in December 1999 were also the result of a $500 million Chinese loan. After leaving the central bank following two maximum stints, Husain did not rest and contributed to improving economic governance and civil service reforms.

November 2026, in the words of SBP Governor Jameel Ahmad, "Pakistan's economic situation remains challenging". While praising the innumerable achievements of Husain, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb said that, as chairman of the Cabinet Committee on State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs), he took inspiration from Husain's reports.

"I have to admit that I took his report as a starting point, but we still have a long way to go, and some of the folks are not happy with that," said Aurangzeb while eulogising the role of the former central bank governor and former adviser to the PM on institutional reforms.

The Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI) on Tuesday awarded Husain the Lifetime Achievement Award in recognition of his public services that began in 1964 as Pakistan's civil servant. He remained the SBP governor from 1999 to the end of 2005, head of many government committees, adviser to the PM and also served in the World Bank.

However, three events – the 1999 economic crisis, the turnaround by 2005 and the persistence of same economic challenges today – underscore that Pakistan produced many great personalities, including Dr Ishrat Husain, but the country remains in the same quagmire with brief intervals of a booming economy.

As part of the World Bank management, Husain advised three countries: Ghana, Tajikistan and Azerbaijan. Ghana was the first country that embraced the World Bank's structural reforms, and it is today a success story, Husain said.

However, Pakistan has taken an unlimited number of World Bank structural reform loans and 25 IMF programmes, but it is still struggling to implement basic reforms that could put the country on a sustainable development path.

Husain said that he helped Tajikistan as the World Bank country director to raise funds for development, which the Tajik leadership still acknowledges, and he was really proud of it.

He said that he advised Azerbaijan to set up a sovereign wealth fund to save the windfall gains from gas sales, and today the state-run sovereign fund had $75 billion of assets.

However, Pakistan established a sovereign wealth fund in 2023 but it had not been able to make the fund operational amid IMF concerns.

"Husain is an institution in himself who turned around the central bank and many other institutions," said Sultan Ali Alana, Chairman Habib Bank Limited.

"The SBP is the best regulator of Pakistan, which was only possible because of the transformational role played by Husain," remarked Finance Minister Aurangzeb.

"Husain is an expert in economy, education, trade and governance reform, and he was Google for us when Google was not that popular in Pakistan," said Dr Abid Qaiyum Suleri, the head of SDPI.

"Retirement is not in the DNA of Dr Ishrat Husain," Aurangzeb said, adding that after leaving the SBP, Husain put a lot of good and hard work into governance reform reports.

"Everyone who comes here in SBP is always in a great hurry, and he will too reconcile with ground realities," were the first remarks by the then deputy governor when he received the news of Husain's appointment in December 1999, revealed incumbent Governor Jameel Ahmad. He said that within six years, Husain transformed the central bank and introduced many reforms.

"Institutional builders must be such that the institution remains the same after they leave," said Ishrat Husain. In his message to the youth, he said "your beginning need not to determine your destination" while sharing his journey from a shy and underdeveloped boy to a towering figure who made his mark in every field where he performed.

Former secretary to the prime minister Nargis Sethi recalled working closely with him during his tenure as chairman of the National Commission for Government Reform, established by the government in 2006.

Dean Emeritus and Professor at Boston University's Pardee School of Global Studies, Dr Adil Najam, said this aspect of his legacy was often underestimated because attention largely remained focused on his achievements as a policymaker.

article_html:
ISLAMABAD:

December 1999, Pakistan had been left with only $300 million in foreign exchange reserves due to crippling economic sanctions and international isolation and at that time military ruler General Pervez Musharraf appointed Dr Ishrat Husain to turn around the central bank.

Six years later, when he left, the country had $13 billion in foreign exchange reserves, also built by purchasing dollars, and people's trust in banks and in the economy had been restored.

The $300 million reserves that Pakistan had in December 1999 were also the result of a $500 million Chinese loan. After leaving the central bank following two maximum stints, Husain did not rest and contributed to improving economic governance and civil service reforms.

November 2026, in the words of SBP Governor Jameel Ahmad, "Pakistan's economic situation remains challenging". While praising the innumerable achievements of Husain, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb said that, as chairman of the Cabinet Committee on State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs), he took inspiration from Husain's reports.

"I have to admit that I took his report as a starting point, but we still have a long way to go, and some of the folks are not happy with that," said Aurangzeb while eulogising the role of the former central bank governor and former adviser to the PM on institutional reforms.

The Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI) on Tuesday awarded Husain the Lifetime Achievement Award in recognition of his public services that began in 1964 as Pakistan's civil servant. He remained the SBP governor from 1999 to the end of 2005, head of many government committees, adviser to the PM and also served in the World Bank.

However, three events – the 1999 economic crisis, the turnaround by 2005 and the persistence of same economic challenges today – underscore that Pakistan produced many great personalities, including Dr Ishrat Husain, but the country remains in the same quagmire with brief intervals of a booming economy.

As part of the World Bank management, Husain advised three countries: Ghana, Tajikistan and Azerbaijan. Ghana was the first country that embraced the World Bank's structural reforms, and it is today a success story, Husain said.

However, Pakistan has taken an unlimited number of World Bank structural reform loans and 25 IMF programmes, but it is still struggling to implement basic reforms that could put the country on a sustainable development path.

Husain said that he helped Tajikistan as the World Bank country director to raise funds for development, which the Tajik leadership still acknowledges, and he was really proud of it.

He said that he advised Azerbaijan to set up a sovereign wealth fund to save the windfall gains from gas sales, and today the state-run sovereign fund had $75 billion of assets.

However, Pakistan established a sovereign wealth fund in 2023 but it had not been able to make the fund operational amid IMF concerns.

"Husain is an institution in himself who turned around the central bank and many other institutions," said Sultan Ali Alana, Chairman Habib Bank Limited.

"The SBP is the best regulator of Pakistan, which was only possible because of the transformational role played by Husain," remarked Finance Minister Aurangzeb.

"Husain is an expert in economy, education, trade and governance reform, and he was Google for us when Google was not that popular in Pakistan," said Dr Abid Qaiyum Suleri, the head of SDPI.

"Retirement is not in the DNA of Dr Ishrat Husain," Aurangzeb said, adding that after leaving the SBP, Husain put a lot of good and hard work into governance reform reports.

"Everyone who comes here in SBP is always in a great hurry, and he will too reconcile with ground realities," were the first remarks by the then deputy governor when he received the news of Husain's appointment in December 1999, revealed incumbent Governor Jameel Ahmad. He said that within six years, Husain transformed the central bank and introduced many reforms.

"Institutional builders must be such that the institution remains the same after they leave," said Ishrat Husain. In his message to the youth, he said "your beginning need not to determine your destination" while sharing his journey from a shy and underdeveloped boy to a towering figure who made his mark in every field where he performed.

Former secretary to the prime minister Nargis Sethi recalled working closely with him during his tenure as chairman of the National Commission for Government Reform, established by the government in 2006.

Dean Emeritus and Professor at Boston University's Pardee School of Global Studies, Dr Adil Najam, said this aspect of his legacy was often underestimated because attention largely remained focused on his achievements as a policymaker.
